extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and students of poetry/creative writing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on creating and evaluating 'poetical' descriptions and the poetical picturesque — how imagery should be composed, how persons are represented in fiction vs poetry, and what makes a description vivid to the mind's eye.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fictional portrait vs plain narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: In literary fiction individuals can seldom be exhibited exactly such as they are; the subtle interminglings of good and evil in actual characters are too fine and subtle for dramatic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For presenting a person 'as he truly is' prefer plain narrative that shows the mind through the events and circumstances that produced it. When a real person is transposed into the novelist's or dramatist's framework, the result often becomes 'another thing' — potentially conveying broad human truth but misrepresenting the particular individual. Anti-pattern: treating a dramatic/novelistic portrait as if it were a faithful documentary likeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetical descriptions focus on elevated/poetic aspects
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetical descriptions are, for the most part, mere views of a character in its elevated and poetic aspects—tributes of admiration to its beautiful qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing poetic description, select and emphasize the elevated, idealized, or beautiful features rather than attempting a forensic, whole-life likeness. Use as tribute or emblem rather than exhaustive biography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lessing's criterion of the poetical picturesque
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet writes picturesquely not when his words furnish materials for a material painting, but when they have the same effect as a material painting — bringing a sensuous object vividly before the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for language that produces the mental effect of a painting: vivid, sensuous, and immediate. Do not confuse literal paintability with the mental vividness required for picturesqueness. Example: Milton's lines may not be paintable yet faithfully convey sensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present a complete object of sight (the 'single-composite-image' rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: A poetic description properly presents a complete object of sight, containing neither more nor less than we might see at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose images so the reader's eye can 'embrace the whole at once' — a self-contained visual unit that functions as an emblem of sentiment or as a compressed narrative. Anti-pattern: overloading a single image with too many disparate elements; conversely, offering fragments that fail to cohere into a single apprehensible scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image-as-emblem and image-as-narrative-device
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet makes the pictured object the emblem of a sentiment instead of explaining the sentiment directly, or tells a story by means of the picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the image to imply or embody feeling and/or narrative development rather than spelling out emotional states or plot. This indirectness increases depth and potency in poetic description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise, rapid, vehement picture-drawing
rubrics_metrics.description: This sort of picture-drawing belongs to rapid, vehement writers; it speeds on the representation and has an oriental heat and intensity about it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For intense, immediate effect favor brisk, concentrated phrasing and energetic cadence. Such picture-drawing benefits from momentum and compressed force; avoid languid or diffused exposition when aiming for this effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paintability is not required
rubrics_metrics.description: The capability of being actually painted is not the criterion of the poetical picturesque; many fine poetic pictures could not be materially painted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not judge a poetic image by whether a painter could depict it; judge by whether the mind's eye can apprehend it with vividness. Examples cited: Pindar and Dante contain 'unpicturable' yet vivid images (darkness, supernatural forms) that succeed in the imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vividness despite unpicturable conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenes unsuitable for literal depiction (e.g., night-darkness, supernatural apparitions) can still be vividly conveyed to the mind's eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ sensory detail, metaphor, and concentrated phrasing to render even 'dark' or abstract scenes immediate. Use details that the imagination can synthesize rather than attempting literal depiction of the impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of the poetic image to its cultural/genre register
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain kinds of images (e.g., grand, universal panoramas in epic) may be less 'picturable' yet true to their poetic function; conversely, picture-drawing suits particular poetic temperaments (e.g., Pindaric or lyric instances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match image scope and method to the poem's genre and voice: world-poems may require universal, less-picturable formulations; lyric or dramatic moments benefit from concentrated, emblematic images. Anti-pattern: forcing a single pictorial method across mismatched poetic projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and unity in poetic detail
rubrics_metrics.description: It is enough that our eye in thought can embrace the whole at once; the poet should not include more or less than the single mental vision allows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise economy: select only the details necessary to form the unitary image. Unity of impression is more important than exhaustive cataloguing. Over-detail diffuses effect; under-detail leaves the image vague.
